Verdict: ACCEPTI find no concrete counterexample to the branched compensation theorem or to the stated unbounded-charge construction, under the hypotheses you explicitly carry forward:the earlier receiver-locality and terminal-tile-ownership lemmas;the all-phase two-leg charge table;the uniform two-leg freezing result;the occupied-degree-three criterion saying that a unique perfect matching rules out every feasible mixed promotion bundle;the stated port-only splice rule;complete endpoint-component receivers and the closed corrected-charge identity.The package does establish two different facts:the proposed constant ceiling on the corrected charge of a fully frozen occupied-degree-three receiver is false; and  the coefficient-one compensation inequality remains valid for the admissible module class.The first failure does not imply a failure of the second.There is one scope boundary that should remain explicit: the reservation corollary uses the earlier global residual-slot first-failure classification. It does not by itself prove a receiver-labelled Hall or ownership flow theorem. Under the global interpretation used in the earlier  $q=5$  result, the corollary is valid.1. Branched splice additivity is validLet  $R_i$ ,  $t_i$ , and  $m_i=|M_i|$  denote the isolated receiver, its selected-vertex count, and its matching-edge count for module  $i$ .The receiver-locality lemma gives the essential ownership fact. A selected support of module  $i$  already has its own endpoint neighbor. If it survived in a tile belonging only to another module’s receiver, it would either have no endpoint in that tile, contradicting locality, or it would see a foreign endpoint in addition to its own, violating selected feasibility. Therefore retained supports do not spill into foreign-only receiver tiles.For a physical tile containing endpoints from several modules, the endpoint set in the tile is connected by the terminal tile-ownership lemma. Each module has at most one port in that tile because its ports are at Manhattan distance at least three, while a  $2\times2$  tile has diameter two. The one-use condition on ports means that the contracted module-incidence graph in that tile has degree at most one at every module vertex.A connected graph of maximum degree one is either a single vertex or one edge. Thus a shared receiver tile contains exactly two modules and exactly one intratile splice. This conclusion is local to the tile. It does not constrain the degree of a module in the global module graph, and it remains true when the global module graph branches or contains cycles.If  $s$  is the number of intratile splice tiles, then:
$$|R_{\mathrm{union}}|=\sum_i |R_i|-s.$$
Each intratile splice removes one selected support from each of its two modules, and both of those supports were counted in their isolated receiver counts by locality. Hence
$$|T\cap V(R_{\mathrm{union}})|
   =\sum_i t_i-2s.$$
An intertile splice removes no support that was counted in the support’s own isolated receiver: the support’s own endpoint lies in a different tile, so locality would otherwise fail. Matching edges are the disjoint union of the module matchings. Therefore
$$\begin{aligned}
\rho_{\mathrm{union}}
 &=\left(\sum_i t_i-2s\right)+\sum_i m_i
      -2\left(\sum_i |R_i|-s\right)\\
 &=\sum_i\left(t_i+m_i-2|R_i|\right)\\
 &=\sum_i\rho_i.
\end{aligned}$$
This is the original corrected receiver charge. No raw overlapping-tile charge is being added.The endpoint-degree statement also survives the splice. At a port, one selected occupied neighbor is replaced at the same physical site by a foreign endpoint. All other occupied neighbors are unchanged, so every endpoint retains occupied degree three.2. The donor injection works even inside one receiverOnly positive two-leg modules need donors. The rotor is nonpositive in every phase.For a positive two-leg module, transport the reference configuration
$$x=(3,2),\qquad p=(3,1),\qquad z=(2,3),\qquad q=(1,3)$$
by the corresponding tile-preserving isometry. Here  $x$  is selected,  $p$  is its endpoint anchor,  $q$  is the degree-three endpoint guard, and the four sites form the local donor pattern.The donor survives the allowed joins for the following reasons. $x$  is not one of the two port-support sites. At minimum leg height four it is already two lattice steps from the relevant bottom port, and larger heights increase that separation. The other port is farther away.More structurally, a foreign port cannot be placed at  $x$ :  $x$  already has the nonport endpoint anchor  $p$  as its occupied neighbor, and a foreign endpoint at  $x$  would create a cross-module endpoint edge incident to the nonport  $p$ , forbidden by the port-only splice rule.The guard  $q$  is not a port, so no splice can replace it or alter its three endpoint neighbors.The two corners adjacent to  $x$  cannot become selected or occupied: either would give  $x$  a second occupied neighbor.The opposite corner  $z$  cannot become selected, because it is adjacent to the degree-three guard  $q$ ; a selected vertex there would already have  $q$  plus its own endpoint neighbor.A foreign endpoint at  $z$  would create an endpoint edge incident to the nonport guard  $q$ , again forbidden.Consequently the donor tile  $Q_i$  remains endpoint-free and contains exactly one selected site, namely  $x_i$ . Its residual physical capacity is therefore exactly one.This also proves non-reuse within a single receiver. If two positive modules tried to use the same physical donor tile, that tile would contain two distinct selected sites, contradicting the just-established unit-donor property. Coincident selected sites are separately impossible because each retained support has its own endpoint neighbor, so coincidence would give the common site two occupied endpoint neighbors.Thus the donor tiles are pairwise distinct even when the positive modules lie in the same endpoint component. No exclusion of additional donor rules is needed. One surviving guard donor per positive module is sufficient.Let  $N_+$  be the number of positive modules. Since all other module charges are nonpositive,
$$\sum_H \rho_H\le N_+.$$
Each chosen donor contributes one unit to the endpoint-free deficit  $D$ , and the donors are distinct, so
$$N_+\le D.$$
The closed receiver identity then gives
$$\frac{mn}{2}-|T|-|M|
   =D-\sum_H\rho_H\ge 0,$$
hence
$$|T|+|M|\le \frac{mn}{2}.$$
This argument is independent of whether the module graph is a path, branches, or contains cycles.3. Rotor and two-leg charge counts are consistentFor the rotor, the matching has four edges. Directly inspecting the eight endpoint coordinates gives:phase  $(0,0)$ : five receiver tiles and four receiver selections, hence
$$\rho_{\mathrm{rotor}}=4+4-2\cdot5=-2;$$
each of the other three translation phases: four receiver tiles and four receiver selections, hence
$$\rho_{\mathrm{rotor}}=4+4-2\cdot4=0.$$
So the rotor never contributes positive charge.For a two-leg module, the established all-phase table gives
$$|M|=w+\frac{a+b}{2}-1$$
and isolated charge
$$1,\quad -1,\quad 1-w,\quad 1-w$$
in the four phases. Therefore the only positive module type is the  $+1$  two-leg phase.The four star attachments use tile-preserving phase- $(0,0)$  copies of the two-leg module. The splice pairs are, in the displayed coordinates,
$$(1,2)\!-\!(0,2),\qquad
(2,4)\!-\!(2,5),\qquad
(4,3)\!-\!(5,3),\qquad
(3,1)\!-\!(3,0),$$
with one endpoint from the rotor and one port from an attached two-leg module. Each splice removes two selected supports, one from each incident module.For a star of width  $w$ :rotor:  $r=5$ ,  $t=4$ ,  $m=4$ ;each attached two-leg module:  $r=w/2+5$ ,  $t=8$ ,  $m=w+3$ ;four intratile splices.Therefore
$$|R_{\star}|=5+4\left(\frac w2+5\right)-4=2w+21,$$

$$|T\cap V(R_{\star})|=4+4\cdot 8-2\cdot4=28,$$

$$|M_{\star}|=4+4(w+3)=4w+16.$$
The corrected charge is
$$\rho_{\star}
 =28+(4w+16)-2(2w+21)
 =2.$$
For  $w=6$ , this gives exactly
$$|P|=80,\qquad |M|=40,\qquad |T|=40,$$

$$|R|=33,\qquad |T\cap V(R)|=28,\qquad \rho=2.$$
The stated  $14\times14$  placement is consistent with these values.The physical star is feasible for every even  $w\ge6$ . The four displayed affine maps put the incident legs next to the four rotor ports. The nonincident arms occupy the four outward directions. Direct coordinate comparison shows that the smallest nonincident separations occur at  $w=6$ ; increasing  $w$  extends the outer portions away from the central gap and does not create a new contact. Thus the all-width claim is geometric, rather than an extrapolation from the finite checks.The star is fully frozen. Each primitive module has a unique internal matching. The module-level star is a tree, so each splice edge is a bridge separating two even endpoint sets. A perfect matching cannot use such a bridge: removing it leaves an odd number of vertices on each side. Hence the union matching is globally unique. Since every endpoint has occupied degree three, the established mixed-bundle criterion rules out every nonempty feasible promotion bundle.This already disproves a universal charge ceiling of one in the restricted occupied-degree-three frozen class.4. The chain boundary argument applies at every lengthFor  $w=14$ , the star  $S$  has
$$|P_S|=144,\quad |M_S|=72,\quad |T_S|=40,$$

$$|R_S|=49,\quad |T_S\cap V(R_S)|=28,\quad \rho_S=2.$$
The connector  $C$  is a transformed two-leg module with
$$|P_C|=34,\quad |M_C|=17,\quad |T_C|=10,$$

$$|R_C|=11,\quad |T_C\cap V(R_C)|=4,\quad \rho_C=-1.$$
The connector’s  $-1$  charge is the correct phase- $(0,1)$  two-leg value after the transpose and odd row translation.For the upper junction  $S$ - $C$ , the supplied table gives all occupied sites in the overlapping rows and their one-row halos. Before removing the splice supports: $S$  has endpoint columns  $5,\ldots,9$  in row  $-11$  and selected column  $4$ ; $C$  has endpoint columns  $0,\ldots,4$  in row  $-11$  and selected column  $5$ .Thus the sole cross-module endpoint edge is
$$(-11,5)-(-11,4).$$
The selected supports at the two splice sites are then removed. The retained supports  $(-12,5)$  and  $(-10,4)$  lie on opposite sides of the splice and are not adjacent to an additional occupied site from the other module. The halo rows  $-13$  and  $-9$  contain no further possible contact.The lower junction is the image under
$$V(r,c)=(-35-r,c),$$
using  $V(C)=C$  and  $V(S)=F(S)$ . Thus the same check proves the lower splice.For the  $j$ -th translate,
$$S_j:\quad [-12-40j,\;17-40j],$$

$$C_j:\quad [-25-40j,\;-10-40j].$$
The only overlaps are: $S_j$  with  $C_j$  in the three rows corresponding to the upper table; $C_j$  with  $S_{j+1}$  in the reflected lower junction.Nonneighboring stars and connectors have wide row gaps. Applying the tile-preserving map  $F^j$  repeats the same finite local table at every  $j$ . This proves feasibility and the absence of additional contacts for arbitrary chain length.5. Exact chain charge and the charge-ceiling failureThere are  $k$  stars and  $k-1$  connectors. Each connector has two intratile splices, so the total number of splice-overlap tiles is  $2(k-1)$ .The receiver tile count is
$$\begin{aligned}
|R|
 &=49k+11(k-1)-2(k-1)\\
 &=58k-9.
\end{aligned}$$
The receiver selected count is
$$\begin{aligned}
|T\cap V(R)|
 &=28k+4(k-1)-4(k-1)\\
 &=28k.
\end{aligned}$$
The matching count is
$$|M|=72k+17(k-1)=89k-17.$$
Therefore the original corrected charge is
$$\begin{aligned}
\rho
 &=28k+(89k-17)-2(58k-9)\\
 &=k+1.
\end{aligned}$$
This is unbounded.The total selected count is a different quantity:
$$|T|=46k-6.$$
The corrected charge uses  $28k$ , the number of selections inside the complete receiver, rather than the total  $46k-6$  selections in the ambient rectangle.For  $k=4$ , the exact receiver figures are
$$|P|=678,\qquad |M|=339,\qquad
|T\cap V(R)|=112,\qquad |R|=223,$$
so
$$\rho=112+339-2\cdot223=5.$$
The total selected count is  $178$ , but it is not the number used in the corrected receiver charge.The ambient rectangle has dimensions  $(40k-10)\times30$ , so
$$\frac{mn}{2}=600k-150.$$
With  $|T|=46k-6$ ,  $|M|=89k-17$ , and  $\rho=k+1$ ,
$$D
 =\frac{mn}{2}-|T|-|M|+\rho
 =466k-126.$$
Thus for  $k=4$ ,
$$D=1738.$$
There are  $4k$  positive two-leg modules, so the donor argument supplies at least  $4k$  pairwise distinct unit donors. At  $k=4$ , there are at least sixteen selected donors for a receiver of charge five. This is entirely compatible with the compensation inequality.The construction therefore refutes a constant receiver-charge ceiling while preserving the coefficient-one area inequality.6. Unique matching and mixed-bundle freezing for the chainEach star is a tree of primitive modules, and the connectors make the global primitive module graph
$$S_0-C_0-S_1-C_1-\cdots-C_{k-2}-S_{k-1},$$
with each  $S_j$  itself a rotor with four two-leg leaves. The entire primitive module graph is a tree.Every primitive module has an even number of endpoint vertices and a unique internal perfect matching. Each intermodule splice is a bridge. If a perfect matching used one of these bridges, deleting that edge would leave an odd number of unmatched endpoint vertices on one side of the bridge. Hence no perfect matching uses an intermodule edge.The only possible perfect matching is therefore the union of the prescribed internal module matchings. It is unique globally.All endpoints retain occupied degree exactly three after the splices. The established degree-three uniqueness criterion then excludes every feasible promotion bundle, including bundles containing both endpoint colors or both endpoints of a matching edge. The argument is not restricted to one-color promotions.Thus the chain is fully frozen for every  $k$ , not merely for the finitely tested lengths.7. Reservation consequence and its scopeLet
$$N_+=\text{number of positive modules}.$$
The donor injection gives
$$\sum_H\rho_H\le N_+.$$
After  $B$  distinct valid unit reservations, at most  $B$  of the chosen donor slots can disappear. Therefore at least
$$N_+-B
 \ge \sum_H\rho_H-B
 =q$$
chosen donor slots remain whenever  $q>0$ .For  $q\le4$ , the earlier threshold already rules out a target-preserving local-quota failure. For  $q=5$ , the earlier first-failure classification leaves only the three listed four-vertex motifs, supported on only three or four positive residual tiles. The surviving donor set contains at least five distinct positive residual tiles, so none of those three motifs can be the entire first failure. Hence the  $q\le5$  reservation consequence follows from the earlier global classification.The precise scope is worth preserving. This argument concerns the earlier global residual-slot graph in which a run-copy may use any incident residual slot. It does not prove a stronger receiver-labelled allocation statement in which each charge unit is restricted to slots owned by its particular receiver or branch. Such a statement would require a demand-labelled Hall or flow condition. That stronger locality claim is not needed for the compensation theorem presented here.The package therefore merits ACCEPT as stated.
